items.stem: A team marks items 'done' when code is written but untested and unintegrated. The strongest fix aligned with Scrum is to:

options.text: Strengthen the Definition of Done to include testing and integration
options.rationale: Correct: a robust Definition of Done ensures the Increment is truly usable.

options.text: Remove the Definition of Done to go faster

options.rationale: Vague criteria do not ensure a usable Increment.

items.explanation: Correct: a robust Definition of Done ensures the Increment is truly usable.

items.stem: In test-driven development, the correct order is to:

options.text: Write a failing test, make it pass, then refactor
options.rationale: Correct: red-green-refactor is the TDD cycle.

options.text: Write all code first, then maybe add tests

options.rationale: Refactoring without tests is risky and not TDD.
Skipping tests is the opposite of TDD.

items.explanation: Correct: red-green-refactor is the TDD cycle.

items.stem: Which TWO practices most directly keep an Increment releasable throughout the Sprint? (Select TWO)

options.text: Integrating work continuously to keep the build green
options.rationale: Correct: continuous integration keeps the Increment releasable.

options.text: Automated tests that run on every change
options.rationale: Correct: automated tests catch regressions early.

options.text: Deferring all integration to the last day
options.rationale: Late integration risks a broken Increment.

options.text: Disabling the test suite to speed merges
options.rationale: Disabling tests removes the safety net.

options.text: Keeping one giant branch for months
options.rationale: Long-lived branches delay integration and risk conflicts.

items.explanation: Correct: continuous integration keeps the Increment releasable. Correct: automated tests catch regressions early.
